key_terms.meaning: Software that takes a program written in one form and produces another form of it, such as object code or a printed report.
A language processor that reads a whole source program and produces a target program, usually in machine or assembly form, before anything runs.
A language processor that reads the source (or an intermediate form) and performs the operations directly, statement by statement, instead of producing a target program.
A translator that maps assembly mnemonics and labels into machine instructions and addresses, producing relocatable object code.
A processor that runs before the compiler to expand macros, include header files, and handle conditional compilation.
A program that joins several object files and library routines into one executable image, resolving external references.
The system program that copies the executable image into memory, relocates it if needed, and starts it.
A data structure, used by every phase, that stores each identifier with its type, scope and storage details.
The component that detects, reports and helps recover from errors in each phase so the compiler can continue on the rest of the program.
A pair (token name, optional attribute value) that the lexer returns to the parser, such as id or num.
The actual string of source characters that matches a pattern, for example the characters total in total = 5.
A description, usually a regular expression, of the set of lexemes that belong to one token class.
When two patterns match at the same position, the lexer picks the one that consumes the most characters; ties go to the earlier rule.
An extra character placed at the end of each buffer half so the end-of-buffer test costs one comparison instead of two per character.
An algebraic notation built from symbols, concatenation, union and closure (Kleene star) that describes a set of strings.
A flow-chart with one state per circle and one labelled arrow per input character; a double circle means the token is accepted.
A nondeterministic finite automaton: a finite set of states with transitions that may be labelled ε or allow several moves on the same character.
A deterministic finite automaton: exactly one transition per state and input symbol, so recognition needs no backtracking.
The algorithm that converts an NFA to a DFA by making each DFA state a set of NFA states, using ε-closure and move.
A lexical-analyzer generator: it reads regular-expression rules and actions and writes a C scanner that applies longest match, then earliest rule.

takeaways: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs; an interpreter executes it as it reads, so errors show up at different times.
The phases of a compiler form a pipeline: characters become tokens, tokens become a parse tree, the tree is checked and lowered, and finally target code is emitted.
Only the front end depends on the source language and only the back end depends on the target machine, which is why compilers can be retargeted.
The lexical analyzer hides character-level detail from the parser and returns one token per call, with an attribute when the token has a value.
Two half-buffers with sentinels cut the cost of the end-of-buffer check, which matters because a lexer examines every character once.
Regular expressions specify tokens; finite automata recognise them; the two are tied together by Thompson's construction and subset construction.
An NFA is easy to build from a regular expression, a DFA is fast to run, so scanners are generated by converting NFA to DFA and minimising it.
LEX removes the hand-coding of scanners: rules are tried longest-match first, and conflicts are settled by rule order.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to draw the phase pipeline with the output of each phase, and to work a full regular-expression-to-minimal-DFA example by hand rather than stating results.

bank.q: Draw the phases of a compiler and explain what representation enters and leaves each phase. State where the symbol table and error handler fit.
outline: Block diagram: lexical analyzer, syntax analyzer, semantic analyzer, intermediate code generator, code optimizer, code generator
Input and output of each phase, e.g. character stream to token stream, tokens to parse tree
Symbol table manager accessed by all phases; error handler attached to each phase
Front end versus back end split, and why the split helps retargeting

bank.q: Compare a compiler, an interpreter and an assembler on input, output, and the time at which errors are reported.
outline: Compiler: whole program in, target program out, errors reported before execution
Interpreter: no target program, runs while reading, stops at the first error reached
Assembler: mnemonic to machine instruction, one-to-one mapping plus symbol resolution
Speed of execution versus speed of debugging trade-off, with an example language for each

bank.q: Explain the role of the lexical analyzer. Define token, lexeme and pattern, and illustrate them on a short statement.
outline: Character stream in, token stream out, one token per call to the parser
Definitions of token, lexeme, pattern with an example such as position = initial + rate * 60
Token names with attributes for identifiers and numbers
Reasons to separate scanning from parsing: simpler grammar, efficiency, portability

bank.q: Explain input buffering in a lexical analyzer using two half-buffers and sentinels.
outline: Why per-character I/O is too slow; read a large block at a time
Two buffers of N characters each, refilled alternately
Sentinel at the end of each half, and the two-test versus one-test loop
Pointer movement and the shift of the last few characters when a token crosses a buffer boundary

bank.q: Convert the regular expression (a|b)*abb into an NFA using Thompson's construction, then into a DFA by subset construction. Show the state sets.
outline: Thompson construction with epsilon transitions for union, concatenation and star
ε-closure and move definitions stated
Subset construction table listing each DFA state as a set of NFA states
Final DFA transition table with start state and accepting states marked

bank.q: Given a DFA with unreachable and equivalent states, minimise it using the partition-refinement method and show every round of splitting.
outline: Remove unreachable states first
Initial partition into accepting and non-accepting states
Repeated splitting on transitions into different blocks, table of rounds
Final minimal DFA and a check that the language is unchanged

bank.q: Write a LEX program that counts lines, words and characters, or that prints all identifiers and keywords of a C file. Explain the role of each section.
outline: Definitions section, rules section with regular expressions and actions, user subroutines section
yytext, yyleng, yyin, yylex and the default rule for unmatched characters
Longest match then earliest rule as the conflict rule, illustrated by a rule pair
Compilation with lex and cc, and sample input with expected output

bank.q: Draw transition diagrams for the token classes identifier and unsigned number, and trace them on the input abc123 and 12.5e3.
outline: Start state, letter then letter-or-digit loop, double circle on identifier
Digits, optional fraction and optional exponent for the number class
Character-by-character trace showing the state after each input
Comment on the longest-match rule when both can start at the same character

bank.q: Group the phases of a compiler into passes and into front end and back end, and explain what each grouping buys.
outline: Definition of a pass: one full read of the source or intermediate form
Single-pass versus multi-pass, and why forward references force two passes
Front end: analysis, machine independent; back end: synthesis, machine dependent
Benefit: n languages and m machines need n+m components, not n times m

bank.q: The lexer must choose between two patterns that match at the same position. Discuss the longest-match and rule-order conventions, and compare a generated scanner with a hand-written one.
outline: Why a parser cannot handle keywords versus identifiers; keyword reservation
Longest match, then earliest rule, with the classic if versus ifelse example
Lookahead of one or two characters, and pushback of unread characters
Comparison of LEX-generated scanner and hand-written scanner on speed, maintainability and error messages

bank.q: Compare NFA and DFA as scanner implementations. Why does subset construction sometimes produce an exponentially larger automaton, and what do real tools do about it?
outline: NFA: compact, easy to build from a regular expression, may need backtracking or parallel state sets
DFA: one transition per character, no backtracking, table size grows with states
Subset construction worst case: 2 to the n states; a small illustration of the blow-up
Practical responses: minimise the DFA, compress tables, or simulate the NFA when the DFA is too large

bank.q: Justify separating lexical analysis from syntax analysis. What would a parser lose if it read characters directly?
outline: Token-level grammar is smaller and easier to parse; whitespace and comments are filtered once
Buffering and scanning are performance-critical and belong in one tuned module
Portability: a new machine means a new scanner, not a new parser
Error reporting at character level versus token level, and the interface (token name plus attribute)

bank.q: Design a scanner for a small language using regular expressions, transition diagrams, automata and a generator tool. State each design decision and its justification.
outline: Token list and keyword reservation table in the symbol table
Regular expressions for identifier, number, operator, keyword, comment; regular definitions reused
Transition diagram per token class, combined NFA, subset construction, minimisation
LEX specification with rule order chosen to respect longest match
Testing plan: buffer boundary, unterminated comment, malformed number, error token returned to the parser

glossary.def: A program that translates a whole source program into an equivalent target program before execution.
A program that executes source or intermediate code directly, without first producing a target program.
A translator from assembly language mnemonics and labels to machine code and relocatable addresses.
Other language processors such as the preprocessor, assembler, linker, loader and macro processor.
A text-level processor that expands macros and includes files before the compiler proper sees the source.
A processor that replaces a named macro call by its body, with arguments substituted.
A program that merges object files and library code into one executable and resolves external symbols.
A program that places an executable image in memory, relocates it and transfers control to it.
The relocatable machine-code output of an assembler or compiler, not yet linked into an executable.
The analysis part of a compiler: lexical, syntax and semantic analysis plus intermediate code generation.
The synthesis part of a compiler: optimisation and target code generation for a particular machine.
One complete reading of the source program or its intermediate representation.
The compiler phase that reads characters and returns tokens to the parser, skipping whitespace and comments.
A token name with an optional attribute value, the unit of input to the parser.
The concrete character string in the source that matches a token pattern.
A rule, normally a regular expression, describing all lexemes of one token class.
Extra information attached to a token, such as the value of a number or a pointer to a symbol-table entry.
A special end-of-buffer character that removes one comparison from the per-character scan loop.
A notation using symbols, union, concatenation and closure to describe a set of strings.
A five-tuple of states, alphabet, transitions, start state and accepting states used to recognise regular languages.
The set of states reachable from a state using epsilon transitions only.
The NFA-to-DFA conversion in which each DFA state is a set of NFA states.
Merging indistinguishable DFA states by partition refinement until no block can be split.
A tool that converts regular-expression rules and actions into a C lexical analyzer.

textbooks.title: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools
textbooks.authors: Alfred V. Aho, Monica S. Lam, Ravi Sethi, Jeffrey D. Ullman
textbooks.pointer: Chapter 1 covers language processors and compiler structure; Chapter 3 covers lexical analysis, input buffering, finite automata and LEX.

textbooks.title: Engineering a Compiler
textbooks.pointer: Its scanning chapter covers the lexer, regular expressions, automata and table-driven scanners.

textbooks.title: Compiler Construction: Principles and Practice
textbooks.pointer: The opening chapters build a scanner using transition diagrams and finite automata.
